draft.title: The environment as a market failure
card: Pollution is a negative externality. It is an external cost that falls on third parties, such as people who breathe dirty air. The polluter does not pay it, so it is left out of the market price.
Because the price leaves out the external cost, the price is too low. The market produces more of the polluting good than the social optimum, and so more pollution.
A public good is non-excludable (no one can be stopped from using it) and non-rivalrous (one person's use does not reduce another's). Clean air and a stable climate are examples.
Nobody can be charged for using clean air, so no one has a reason to pay to protect it. Markets therefore tend to overuse the environment and under-protect it.
draft.remember: The market price leaves out the cost of pollution, and no one pays for clean air, so the environment is overused.

a.q: Why does a free market produce too much of a good that pollutes?
opts: The price leaves out the external cost to third parties
Firms must pay for the cost of the pollution they cause
Buyers value the good at less than its social cost
Clean air is rivalrous, so firms compete to use it up
a.why: The polluter does not pay the external cost, so the price is too low and output is above the social optimum. Firms do not pay for the pollution, which is why the market does not limit it.
a.clue: Who pays for the harm caused by pollution?

b.q: A steelworks in Port Kembla releases fumes that make nearby residents ill. Its steel price covers only its own costs. What does this show about the market for steel?
opts: It overproduces, because the price ignores the health cost
It underproduces, because residents gain no benefit
It hits the social optimum, because buyers accept the price
It cannot trade, because clean air is non-excludable
b.why: The health cost falls on residents, who are third parties, so it is not in the price. The price is too low and the market produces more steel than the social optimum. Clean air being non-excludable explains why it is overused, but it does not stop steel being sold.
b.clue: Does the steel price include the cost borne by residents?

a.best: The price leaves out the external cost to third parties
also_right: Buyers value the good at less than its social cost

b.best: It overproduces, because the price ignores the health cost

problems.detail: The distractor 'Buyers value the good at less than its social cost' is defensibly true. At the market output, the marginal benefit to buyers is below the marginal social cost, which is what overproduction means. A careful student could pick it. Reword it so it is clearly false, for example 'Buyers value the good at more than its social cost'.
Port Kembla has essentially one steelworks (BlueScope), so the stem reads as a factual claim that a real firm's fumes make residents ill. Use an unnamed or fictional location to keep it hypothetical.
